I want to share some deep observations and testing results regarding this issue. I've spent considerable time debugging why Qwen-Max (specifically `qwen3-max-2026-01-23` accessed via API) fails to maintain a natural thinking process in OpenCode, especially when dealing with non-English languages.

**Methodology & Testing Environment:**
To isolate the root cause, I rebuilt OpenCode from source on Arch Linux using a custom PKGBUILD. I conducted tests across the following variables:
1. **System Prompts:** I stripped the default prompt (`default.txt`) of all restrictive instructions like *"fewer than 4 lines"*, *"Output text to communicate with the user...". I even translated the entire system prompt to Russian to anchor the context.
2. **Temperature:** I found that OpenCode hardcodes the temperature to `0.55` for any model ID containing "qwen" ( `src/provider/transform.ts`). I removed this hardcode during compilation to ensure the model runs at its native/optimal temperature for reasoning.
3. **Language & Mode:** Tested English vs. Russian, with `thinking` enabled vs. disabled.
4. **Model Comparison:** Compared `qwen-max` against `qwen-plus` under the exact same API and OpenCode environment.

**Key Observations:**
1. **Thinking Disabled:** Without the CoT (Chain-of-Thought) block, `qwen-max` works perfectly fine and generates excellent responses in both English and Russian.
2. **Thinking Enabled (English):** The thinking chain is noticeably truncated. It works, but it's significantly shorter and less explorative compared to running the same model in OpenWebUI with a clean system prompt.
3. **Thinking Enabled (Russian):** This is where the model completely collapses. The grammar breaks, words are misspelled, and it often forgets to close the `</think>` tag. It looks like the attention mechanism breaks down completely.
4. **The `qwen-plus` Exception:** Interestingly, `qwen-plus` does *not* suffer from this issue at all. Under the exact same OpenCode conditions, `qwen-plus` generates massive, detailed thinking chains, seamlessly mixing Russian and English in the `<think>` block, and outputs perfect results.

**The Theory: "Negative Jailbreak" via Tool Instructions**
OpenCode doesn't just send the `default.txt` prompt. It dynamically injects massive amounts of strict English instructions for every tool available to the agent ( `bash.txt`,  `todowrite.txt`,  `task.txt`, etc.). These files are filled with strict imperatives: *"be concise"*, *"never write extra text"*, *"only output JSON"*.

Because `qwen-max` is an extremely highly-aligned model (optimized to follow system instructions flawlessly), it suffers from a **"Negative Jailbreak"**. 
It attempts to apply OpenCode's strict brevity rules *inside* the `<think>` block. The model experiences severe cognitive dissonance: its architecture demands expansive reasoning, but the system prompt demands extreme conciseness. When you add the cognitive load of reasoning in a non-English language, the model's attention collapses entirely.

On the other hand, `qwen-plus` (likely due to its multimodal training and larger 1M context window) seems to naturally separate these constraints, applying OpenCode's strict rules *only to the final output*, leaving the `<think>` block free and unconstrained.

For all people coming across this. Claude models do still work when connected via third party subscriptions. Personally highly recommend the Github Copilot Subscription (officially supports opencode - https://github.blog/changelog/2026-01-16-github-copilot-now-supports-opencode/ with 300 or 1500 requests depending on the subscription tier) using github-copilot/claude-sonnet-4.6 (usage multiplier x1) for Sisyphus (Oh my openagent or short OMO opencode plugin) and for smaller tasks github-copilot/claude-haiku-4.5 (usage multiplier x0.33; librarian role within OMO etc.).

Just an FYI - I dug into this a while back. I am not sure why it gets tagged as IOAccelerator but the actual references are all string related and don't appear to be truly GPU related.

I used a version of bun with debug symbols and tracked allocations back to sources and almost all of it was related to string handling stuff.

Fair points, and I appreciate the honest take.

The €1 is really just a way to measure whether the features I'm building actually matter to people — it's signal, not a paywall. If I open-sourced the fork right now, the ideas would get absorbed into other tools overnight and I'd lose the only feedback loop I have for knowing what's worth pursuing.

Think about it from the other side: if I pushed all my tweaks as a public OpenCode fork, what happens? Either they get cherry-picked into a dozen projects within a week with zero attribution, or they sit ignored. Neither tells me anything useful.
Keeping it closed for now lets me iterate fast, validate what works, and then contribute back the things that proved valuable — not just dump half-baked experiments on the community. That said, nothing I'm building exists without OpenCode.

I get that closed-source rubs people the wrong way, but building on top of open-source and charging for added value is how most of the tools we use every day work — and the MIT license exists precisely to allow that.

I took a stab at this with draft PR #19136, but after manual testing I found the fix doesn't actually solve the problem for the default configuration.

**What the PR does:** Adds a `Skill.invalidate()` method that clears the cached skills, and wires it to `FileWatcher.Event.Updated` so that editing a SKILL.md triggers a cache reload. The Command cache also rebuilds when skills are invalidated.

**Why it doesn't work in practice:** `FileWatcher` only watches `Instance.directory` when `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FILEWATCHER=true` (see `src/file/watcher.ts:123`). Without that flag, only `.git/HEAD` is watched, so `FileWatcher.Event.Updated` never fires for SKILL.md changes. Most users won't have the experimental flag enabled.

There's also a secondary gap: even with the flag on, the watcher only covers CWD. Skills loaded from parent directories (monorepo `.claude/skills/`) or global directories (`~/.claude/skills/`) wouldn't trigger invalidation.

**The cache invalidation logic itself works** — `Skill.invalidate()` correctly clears the cache and the next `Skill.all()`/`Skill.get()` call re-reads from disk. All automated tests pass. The gap is in how invalidation gets triggered.

**Possible approaches a maintainer might consider:**

1. **Dedicated watcher for skill directories** — After the initial skill load, set up `fs.watch` or parcel watcher subscriptions on just the known skill directories (`state.dirs`). Independent of the experimental flag.
2. **Poll-based mtime checks** — On each `ensure()` call, `stat` the loaded SKILL.md files and invalidate if any mtime has changed. Simple but adds disk I/O per call.
3. **Broaden the experimental watcher scope** — Extend `FileWatcher` to also cover skill directories when enabled, and eventually promote it out of experimental.

Happy to update the PR if a maintainer has a preferred direction.

Ran into the same issue running like this:
```docker run -ti --rm  -v ~/.local/share/opencode:/root/.local/share/opencode  opencode-dev```

Attempted out of the box sqllite `.recover` which restored session and part tables but the message table pages were on the corrupted blocks and came back empty - leaving me with historical session but ZERO conversation history! no good. 

Was able to start a new opencode database and Opus 4.6 figured out how to actually surigicall reconstruct messages from the parts table.  [Here is the script ](https://gist.github.com/etherops/df78300a0ce6eeb08e056533bdfa30d9) it came up with in case someone else needs this workaround.  good luck we're all counting on you.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
     
https://gist.github.com/etherops/df78300a0ce6eeb08e056533bdfa30d9

My suggestions if you run into this and `.recover` isn't good enough, blow away and get a fresh opencode database and give it that python code as guidance instead of trying to run this on your system which will break obv due to hard coded filenames etc. 

Notes:
* Swap gotchas: don't replace opencode.db while opencode is running, and delete -shm/-wal alongside the swap.
* if you manually reconstruct messages without including modelID, providerID, mode, agent, and path in the data JSON, opencode crashes on load with undefined is not an object (evaluating 'str3.replace').
